chantedPrayers.text: Liberating Prayer O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha, precious Treasury of Compassion, Bestower of Supreme Inner Peace. You who love all beings without exception are the source of happiness and goodness, and you guide us to the liberating path. Your body is a wish-fulfilling jewel, your speech is supreme, purifying nectar, and your mind is refuge for all living beings. With folded palms I turn to you, Supreme unchanging Friend. I request from the depths of my heart, please give me the light of your wisdom to dispel the darkness of my mind and to heal my mental continuum. Please nourish me with your goodness, that I in turn may nourish all beings with an unceasing banquet of delight. Through your compassionate intention, your blessings and virtuous deeds, and my strong wish to rely upon you, may all suffering quickly cease and all happiness and joy be fulfilled, and may holy Dharma flourish forevermore. Going for Refuge I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. Generating Bodhichitta Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Four Immeasurables May everyone be happy, May everyone be free from misery, May no one ever be separated from their happiness, May everyone have equanimity, free from hatred and attachment. Visualizing the Field for Accumulating Merit In the space before me is the living Buddha Shakyamuni, surrounded by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, like the full moon surrounded by stars. Prayer of Seven Limbs With my body, speech, and mind, humbly I prostrate, and make offerings both set out and imagined. I confess my wrong deeds from all time and rejoice in the virtues of all. Please stay until samsara ceases and turn the Wheel of Dharma for us. I dedicate all virtues to great enlightenment. Offering the Mandala The ground sprinkled with perfume and spread with flowers, The Great Mountain, four lands, sun and moon, Seen as a Buddha Land and offered thus, May all beings enjoy such Pure Lands. The objects that give rise to my attachment, hatred, and confusion, my friends, enemies, and strangers, our bodies and enjoyments — please accept these and bless me to be released directly from the three poisons. IDAM GURU RATNA MANDALAKAM NIRYATAYAMI. Prayer of the Stages of the Path The path begins with strong reliance On my kind Teacher, source of all good; O Bless me with this understanding To follow him with great devotion. This human life with all its freedoms, Exceedingly rare and most meaningful — O Bless me with this understanding All day and night to seize its essence. My body, like a water bubble, Decays and dies so very quickly; After death come results of karma, Just as the shadow of a body. With this firm knowledge and remembrance Bless me to be extremely cautious, Always avoiding harmful actions And gathering abundant virtue. Samsara’s pleasures are deceptive, Give no contentment, only torment; So please bless me to strive sincerely To gain the bliss of perfect freedom. O Bless me so that from this pure thought Come great unfailing conscientiousness, To keep as my essential practice The Dharma’s root, the Pratimoksha. Just like myself, all my kind mothers Are drowning in samsara’s ocean; O So that I may soon release them, Bless me to train in bodhichitta. But I cannot become a Buddha By this alone without three ethics; So bless me with the strength to practise The Bodhisattva’s ordination. By pacifying my distractions And analyzing perfect meanings, Bless me to quickly gain the union Of special insight and quiescence. When I become a pure container Through the common path, bless me to enter The essence practice of good fortune, The supreme vehicle, the Tantra. The two attainments both depend on My sacred vows and my commitments; Bless me to understand this clearly And keep them at the cost of my life. By constant practice in four sessions, The way explained by holy Teachers, O Bless me to gain both the stages Which are the essence of the Tantras. May those who guide me on the good path And my companions all have long lives; Bless me to pacify completely All obstacles, outer and inner. May I always find perfect Teachers And take delight in holy Dharma, Accomplish all grounds and paths swiftly, And gain the state of Vajradhara. Receiving Blessings From the hearts of all the holy beings, streams of light and nectar flow down, granting blessings and purifying.

guidedMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
guidedMeditation.text:
Meditation can begin by generating the power of regret. We can look at some challenge or problem in our life and identify that this is arising strictly due to negative karma created in the past. There is no other cause.

We can think, how is it that harmful results follow from harmful actions? It is through the force of an imprint placed on our mind that the potential to experience future suffering comes about. For example, a person who commits murder plants a very strong negative impression on his or her mind. That impression or seed carries with it the potential to place that mind in a state of extreme misery. Unless the impression of that non-virtuous action is purified, this latent seed will remain in the mind, its power dormant but unimpaired. When the appropriate circumstances are eventually met, the potential power of this impression will be activated. The seed will ripen as an experience of intense suffering — for instance, as rebirth in a karmically created realm of hellish misery. Just contemplate and acknowledge that whatever problem we are experiencing is 100% arising due to karma created in the past.

The situation is analogous to that of an arid piece of ground into which seeds were planted a long time ago. As long as these seeds are not somehow destroyed, they will retain their potential to grow. Should the ground be watered sufficiently, these long-forgotten seeds will suddenly sprout forth. In a similar fashion, our karmic actions plant their seeds in the field of our consciousness. When we encounter the proper conditions, these seeds will sprout and bear their karmic fruit.

Through acknowledging that the suffering we are experiencing is just coming from negative karma, we can infer there are also other countless negative karmic seeds in our mind, and that if these are not purified, they will definitely lead to various forms of suffering. In order to develop a strong determination: I do not want these karmic seeds to ripen, therefore I must purify them completely. When we generate this intention, we can hold it single-pointedly in our heart.

Then, finally, we can just briefly reflect on our meditation break practice from the last week. Just check — how did it go, remembering Dharma in daily life? Were we able to remember, and why? Or did we forget, and if so, why? Just check very honestly and gently, and come to some conclusion about our meditation break practice. And with this conclusion in our heart, we can gradually arise from our practice.

shantiDevaReading.text:
Therefore from today I go for refuge to the Conqueror Buddhas who protect living beings, who seek to give refuge to all living beings, and who with their great strength eradicate all fear. Likewise, I sincerely go for refuge to the Dharma they have realized, which dispels the fears of samsara, and to the assembly of Bodhisattvas.

Overcome with fear, I offer myself to Arya Samantabhadra, and I offer my body into the service of Arya Manjushri. To Protector Avalokiteshvara, who acts unerringly out of compassion, I utter this desperate cry for help: Oh, please protect me, an evildoer. Seeking refuge from my heart, I pray to Arya Akashagarbha, to Arya Ksitigarbha, and to all the compassionate protectors.

I go for refuge to Arya Vajrapani, upon sight of whom all harmful beings such as the messengers of the Lord of Death flee in terror to the four directions. Previously I transgressed your advice, but now, having seen these great dangers, I go to you for refuge to quickly dispel my fears.

If I need to follow the doctor’s advice when frightened by an ordinary illness, how much more necessary is it to follow Buddha’s advice when perpetually afflicted by the many harmful diseases of the delusions? If all the people living in this world can be greatly harmed by just one of these delusions, and if no medicine other than Dharma can be found anywhere to cure them, those who do not act in accordance with the Dharma teachings given by Buddha, the all-knowing physician, through which all pains of the delusions can be removed, are surely foolish and confused.

If it is necessary to exercise caution when near a small ordinary precipice, how much more necessary is it when near the fathomless pits of hell into which I could fall for a very long time? It is unwise to indulge in pleasures thinking, at least I shall not die today, for without doubt the time will come when I shall become nothing.

Who will grant me fearlessness? How can I be freed from these fears? If I shall inevitably become nothing, how can I continue to indulge?

What remains with me now from the pleasant experiences of my previous lives that have now ceased, and yet because of my strong attachment to worldly pleasures I have gone against the advice of my spiritual guide? If, when I depart from this life and from my friends and relatives, I must wander all alone, why commit non-virtue for the sake of friends and enemies? How can I definitely be freed from non-virtue, the source of all suffering?

Throughout the day and the night, I should think only about this. Whatever I have done, out of unknowing and confusion, be it a natural non-virtue, or a transgression — with my palms pressed together, and my mind fearful of suffering, prostrating myself again and again, I confess them all before the protectors.

I request all the holy beings to free me from all my evils and faults, and since these bring only harmful results, in future I will not commit them again.

dataShares.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dataShares.text:
It’s just so important to mix our Dharma practice in our daily life, and to use all the things that happen, especially when we’re really meditating on Lam Rim. We have tons of daily appearances that keep occurring, and if we look closely, everything is a teaching about Lam Rim. And when we look at our life that way, we’ll keep a peaceful, happy mind all day, and our whole life will be filled with Lam Rim.

Like when I was out for a walk this morning, there’s a sign — I forget what street it is, but between 3rd and 4th — a huge sign that says, “No more death.” And I was thinking, yes! No more uncontrolled death. That’s the renunciation teaching. No more contaminated death. But I noticed it was a bunch of children on the mural, and it’s basically all these kids that got ran over and died in that area. So it’s like a road safety sign or mural. I’ve seen it before, but it just struck me a little bit differently today, thinking about renunciation. Just to think — there’s never going to be no more death in samsara.

Or maybe you’re watching the World Cup, which is on right now, which is inspiring in a lot of ways, but you can also think of all these countries where there’s a team coming to play — some of them are in absolute chaos, full of death and destruction. Some of these players that are coming are from the regimes who are creating the death and destruction. So it’s not that pretty, actually, in some ways. We need to use these appearances and see things through the lens of Lam Rim. Because the teachings are everywhere for us to see. If we do that, our Lam Rim practice will be so alive and vibrant. We’ll get many blessings from this kind of consideration.

dataShares.speaker: Sumit
dataShares.text:
Someone very near and dear to me — it’s uncertain, but probably they’re going to for the most part disappear from my life. And so I’m very bothered by this. And of course I have all these Dharma tools and things like this, and none of that stuff is really landing. And then I was talking to a friend, and one of my friends said, “You need to grieve this.” And when that rung true to me, I was like, yeah — that’s like how I honor this. It seems like I should grieve this and suffer this loss. And it’s not appropriate for me to find peace. And that’s why none of the Dharma is landing — because I actually don’t want to feel peaceful, I want to feel the sorrow.

So my question is — of course when we talk about Dharma, Buddha is saying we should be peaceful all the time. But sometimes when something really bad happens, is that true? Maybe there is this feeling of, I should feel sorrow. But maybe not.

dataShares.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dataShares.text:
Yeah, I’m sorry, Sumit — that’s not a fun experience to have. Someone dear and close to us getting sort of cut out, or cutting themselves out, from our life.

These kind of things have a tricky quality, because in the end, we’re definitely going for peace, and we’re definitely going for using Dharma to get to that peace. So 100% we’re going there. It’s just the way that we go there is the thing that’s tricky.

If we think about Dharma as a medicine for an illness, every Dharma teaching is designed to be taken as practical advice — it’s like a certain prescription for a different ailment. As we start practicing, we have our original set of mental ailments, and usually the reason we stick around is that we get some prescriptions that address those ailments. But there’s still a whole host of other types of mental ailments that maybe we didn’t bring with us into the teachings originally. And what often happens is that the kind of problems we bring into the Dharma, and the teachings that solve those problems, become our sort of little repertoire.

What can happen is that our mind becomes a little bit used to those tools, because they solve the problems we brought with us. But we kind of forget there’s 84,000 tools, and that means there’s also 84,000 permutations of delusion — 21,000 anger permutations, 21,000 attachment permutations, 21,000 ignorance permutations, and 21,000 cocktails of the three.

So what often happens is we can prune the other Dharma teachings and practices, because we didn’t necessarily have the specific delusion problem they solve. Then when that problem comes along, we go into our toolbox and each tool doesn’t feel right — it feels phony, fake, like we’re trying to push something down. And it’s not because they don’t work — they’re just tools for different jobs, medicines for different ailments.

In these moments, we have to clear the slate — throw out the defaults and re-look at the problem from a completely fresh mind, as if we’re a new Dharma practitioner bringing that problem to the teacher for the first time.

Then what we’re trying to do is really trace specifically the suffering to the delusion that’s present — not just the delusion itself, but the specific version of it. It’s not sufficient to just say, “Oh, it’s attachment” or “It’s self-cherishing.” What version of it? Is it attachment to reputation? To praise? To pleasure? To not feeling pain? Is it self-cherishing with respect to safety? Feeling superior? Self-righteous? There are all these nuances.

So we take data point one — our raw suffering. There’s a wisdom in what your friend said about feeling the grief. We have to identify that raw suffering, because that’s the key to understanding the delusion. We don’t need to wallow in it — but we do need the raw suffering to trace it to the delusion. It’s the symptom linked to the ailment.

What I found is that if I do this sincerely, it won’t take too long, but there are wrong answers the mind comes up with first — all the things we always go to. Once you exhaust those, you start to get to the actual problem.

Then we apply the opponent — but only on the basis of really wanting to be free of that delusion. If we don’t really want to be free of it yet, that’s its own step — thinking of the faults of that delusion.

Last thing: we say “recognize, reduce, abandon” the delusions. Sometimes people talk about the recognize stage as if we’re being patient with the delusion. That’s completely wrong. We’re patient with ourself, not with delusions. Delusions are enemies designed to destroy us. The recognize stage is identifying the delusion and thinking of its faults — developing a wish to overcome it. It’s not sitting with it and being patient with it.

dataShares.speaker: Sumit
dataShares.text:
This is really helpful. It helps me narrow down my issue more. I’m in step two. I do see the problem. I do see the faults of the delusion. I’m suffering. But I have no admiring faith for the solution. I don’t admire the idea of being peaceful.

It’s like — if I wasn’t attached to this person, I’d be at peace. That doesn’t seem cool to me. That’s where I’m at.

dataShares.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dataShares.text:
That’s a great thing to see. It’s a nuance to what’s going on that wouldn’t be obvious day one. Oh, I have this feeling that it’s wrong to feel at peace in this situation — it’s like a doubt.

Then it would be about, okay, how can I work on that doubt? For example, thinking: my peace is like a vehicle, not a destination. My peace is a way to navigate through the situation — it’s not an end in itself. I’m not just abiding in a place of peace. Peace doesn’t mean that something bad didn’t happen. Being at peace doesn’t mean something bad didn’t happen. I can acknowledge something bad happened and still be at peace. Those aren’t contradictory.

dataShares.speaker: Dale
dataShares.text: This is a follow-up to Sumit’s topic. I’m wondering if it’s possible to be grateful that you had this relationship in your life and also be sad at the same time — until the sadness lessens.

dataShares.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dataShares.text:
Yeah, to be grateful about a relationship but also to be sad until the sadness lessens — that’s a nice approach. There are stories in the scriptures of great yogis passing away and people being distraught that their teachers passed away. What is that? Is it attachment? Is it faith?

Really, with any of these things, it’s just asking: what direction are we going in? With grief — maybe we feel sad, but are we going in the right direction, or are we just plateauing? Is it moving in the right direction, or is it getting worse? And if it’s getting worse, then we need to intervene. If it’s all getting better and moving in the right direction, then we can be patient with that and understand, okay, this is a process and it’s taking time, but I’m moving where I need to go.

dataShares.speaker: Anne K
dataShares.text:
I was really happy when the Eight Worldly Concerns came up last week, because it reminded me of a teaching from our silent retreat last October — it was one of my favorite teachings ever. We talked about how real happiness is inner peace arising from wisdom. And I remember we were talking about everything else being like licking honey off a razor’s edge. And you said, if you’re in a store and there’s two kinds of honey — honey with razors and razor-free honey — why don’t you go for the razor-free honey?

That helped me so much all week with all of my Eight Worldly Concerns and my attachments. I’m like, well, yeah, but then there’s this razor-free honey! It was such a light-hearted, fun teaching, and it was also so clear. Now I can’t get it out of my head, and I just wanted to share it again with everyone.

dataShares.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dataShares.text:
Yeah, that’s great, Anne. That analogy comes from Buddha originally, or Nagarjuna — following attachments is like licking honey off of a razor’s edge. And of course, we want the razor-free honey. It just helps us fall in love with the peace and the bliss of meditation, which is the razor-free honey. And then the more we fall in love with that, the less the razor-filled honey looks attractive to us — which isn’t about suppression. It’s just, we’re not interested, because we’ve got good honey going on.

And it’s a good reminder about the importance of meditative experience, so that we can really find the peace of meditation. Because that’s the proof of our razor-free honey. But it’s hard to get that peace that feels so much more interesting than the objects of attachment without some quiet in meditation.

dataShares.speaker: Fran
dataShares.text:
I inadvertently carried out an experiment on the effects of laziness on my practice. I started off the week feeling great. I had done the two weeks of the Lam Rim group. And I was getting up in the morning and really doing the reading and doing the meditation. I was doing Herchul, which I don’t generally do on a regular basis. And I was embedding a purification practice into it. I felt my practice was going really well. I was thinking about karma and the effects that everything I do has an effect, and really looking at it in everyday life.

And then I woke up one morning and said, “Ah, it’s okay, I’ll do it later.” And all of a sudden, I wasn’t participating in the Lam Rim group, in the WhatsApp group anymore. And it was like, now I’ve missed too much, it’s getting complicated. I didn’t do the reading yet. And then one day I stopped doing the little embedded purification practice. And little by little, it just degraded this whole week. So it’s just a cautionary tale — first of all, not to be prideful in how well it’s going, because it falls apart really easily. And the laziness of attachment is just all over this.

dataShares.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dataShares.text:
Yeah, thanks, Fran. It’s true — those spiritual structures we set up are so important. And the delusions can be so sneaky — they’re deeply rooted in our karma. It is very easy to get a little bit prideful in our practice — not in a haughty way, but just taking it for granted.

These moments are helpful to remind us: my structure is basically the whole thing. This is the thing that’s protecting me and keeping me sane. At some point, I thought, I’m going to evolve out of needing that structure. And I have found absolutely not. Three days or so without it, and I’m feral. It’s kind of scary to see how the delusions are just ready to take over. And one day it won’t be like that, when we realize emptiness directly. But until then, they’re essentially just waiting. They sit there like, okay, we’ll just wait for a bad day.

The practical takeaway is we should really value our spiritual structures, keep them sacred, and protect them. We all learn over time which are the ones that work for us. We do need to experiment a little bit, find something that works. But then when we find what works, it is good to be a bit rigid about protecting them.

dataShares.speaker: Mary Ann
dataShares.text:
I realize this week that my main delusion right now is just distraction. Just pure, unmitigated, constant distraction.

But one of the things that happened this week was this idea that feelings are the end of a karmic effect. That just blows my mind. It’s so 180 to how I’ve always lived my life — I have these feelings, now what am I going to do about them, express them, turn them into something, like art. They’re like the stuff. And so to think that they are the end of something else — maybe I wasn’t really seeing clearly, but the fact that we’re living attached to what we did in the past, it just feels like a ball and chain. Which it is. Because if it’s positive, it’s also generated by a past action.

So I was just kind of trying to — if anyone had any insight about how they take emotions and see them as having a connection to an action, when they just feel so raw and real and present — it’s kind of a question.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: Responding to Mary Ann: Feelings, the five aggregates, and the engine room of samsara
teaching.text:
Feelings are the effect of karma — it’s how karma ripens as a feeling: positive, negative, neutral. One of the principal ways that it ripens.

As Buddha explained the five aggregates — form, feeling, discrimination, compositional factors, consciousness — consciousness is our main mind, form is our body. Compositional factors means everything in our whole being other than feeling and discrimination. So it’s interesting: wow, these two little parts get their own place in our whole being. Our whole basic self is just an “I” imputed on the five aggregates. That’s all self is.

So it’s amazing — just the little part of us that either feels good, bad, or neutral. It’s not even an emotion. It’s not a delusion. It’s just the part of us that is good, bad, or neutral. It’s like a little switch that has three spots. That little bit deserves to be as central as our whole body or our whole mind. Equally important.

Geshe Chekawa’s advice: the three feelings, the three poisons, and the three virtuous roots are basically our entire practice. The three feelings are good, bad, and neutral. Whenever we get a good feeling, we get attached. Whenever we get a bad feeling, we get angry. Whenever we have a neutral feeling, we become ignorant. That’s our whole samsara — just responding to feelings.

And then three virtuous roots — non-attachment, non-hatred, non-ignorance — are basically a way to liberate ourselves. The entirety of our practice can be summarized as just trying not to develop the three poisons when we have those three feelings. That’s the whole practice, kind of. So it’s helpful to make that little tiny part of our mind one of the main places we want to intervene.

Since feeling is just an effect, we don’t need to respond or act on feelings. We’re trained to chase the good feelings and run away from the bad feelings. But we don’t need to. It’s just a habit.

Sometimes what I’ll try to do is just think of the feelings as a little icon on my dashboard. When you’re driving your car and your dashboard is showing some funny thing going on, you don’t need to feel anything about it. You can just go, yeah, that’s a check engine light. I might explode sometime soon, but it might be fine. It’s just a little signal. We don’t need to get emotionally riled up in it. It’s just an ephemeral phenomenon.

In the 12 Dependent-Related Links, feeling is one of the most important parts — one of the engine rooms of samsara.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: MTB paragraphs 381–386: Power of Reliance — going for refuge and bodhichitta
teaching.text:
Power of Reliance. In the next passage, Shantideva, full of regret for his misguided actions, turns to the Three Jewels for refuge from suffering.

I go for refuge to all the Buddhas, those who protect all sentient beings from fear. I go for refuge to the Dharma Jewel that is possessed by these Buddhas. I go for refuge to the Assembly of Superior Bodhisattvas. I go for refuge to you, the Three Jewels, and pray for protection from non-virtue, the cause of rebirth in hell.

These are called the Eight Great Bodhisattvas — kind of Buddha’s main eight disciples. They’re basically Bodhisattvas from other worlds that appeared as Buddha’s main disciples to help spread the Dharma. So Buddha appeared as Buddha, and they appeared as Bodhisattva disciples to help him.

Here Shantideva states that his regrettable non-virtuous actions were all performed because he failed to heed the teachings of the enlightened beings. As purification of all evil depends upon following these teachings sincerely, Shantideva invokes the power of reliance by going for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha from the depths of his heart.

In the Mahayana tradition, the power of reliance refers to going for refuge and generating bodhichitta. If we slip and fall down on the ground, the way we raise ourselves up again is by relying upon that very ground. Similarly, if we wish to raise ourselves up after committing an unskillful action, we do so by relying upon the objects against whom we committed that action. All non-virtue can be included within two categories: non-virtuous actions directed against the Three Jewels, and those directed against sentient beings. Purifying the former entails relying upon refuge. For actions committed against sentient beings, the power of reliance entails regenerating the precious thought of bodhichitta — reminding ourselves that we are seeking enlightenment solely for the sake of those beings we have regrettably harmed.

So it’s like making it right, making our non-virtue right — either by relying on the Buddhas or wanting to purify to help those that we have harmed.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: MTB paragraphs 387–403: Power of the Opponent Force — six methods and the story of Lam Chung
teaching.text:
Power of the Opponent Force. It is this third power, when combined with a deep sense of regret, that will actually purify the effects of our negative actions. There are six types of activity used as opponent forces: reciting the names of Buddhas, reciting mantras, reciting Buddhist Dharma scriptures, meditating on emptiness, making offerings, and constructing or repairing images of a Buddha’s body, speech, and mind.

But there is nothing magical about them. They are only effective when based on a strong foundation of regret and combined with a sincere desire to purify our negativities. If we wish to purify non-virtue, any positive virtuous action can be used as the opponent power. Even sweeping a shrine room, if done with sincere regret and a strong intention to purify, can be a powerful opponent force.

To illustrate this, there is the famous story of Lam Chung. Before he became a monk, he had already gained the unenviable reputation of being dull and unteachable. He was sent to school but expelled because his teacher said he was unable to remember any of his lessons. His parents sent him to his elder brother, Arya Lam Chen, who taught him one verse of Dharma. Lam Chung studied this verse for three months but never mastered it. If he memorized it in the morning, he would forget it by the evening. He recited the verse so often while up in the hills that even the shepherds came to memorize and understand it. But poor Lam Chung still could not master it.

This is like when our family and friends remind us of our Dharma practice. They’re like, “Aren’t you a Buddhist? Aren’t you supposed to be patient?” They’re like the shepherds, and we’re like Lam Chung. We should never resent our family and friends for reminding us about our practice.

Lam Chung was completely desolate. He felt utterly depressed. He thought, now I’m neither a monk nor a layperson. The Buddha saw all that had taken place and asked him why he was crying. In that openness, in that space, we’ll get answers if we’re completely humble.

Buddha taught Lam Chung just two words of Dharma and appointed him as the sweeper at the temple. He swept with great dedication, reciting the few words Buddha had taught him. Through the power of Buddha, whenever Lam Chung swept the right side, more dust would appear on the left side, and vice versa.

In our life, it might not be literal dirt, but there’s situations that happen over and over and over again. It’s saying to us: purify your mind. This will never stop until you purify. Those things that are happening over and over again are our special gifts — to encourage us to purify. Usually people have one main one — it could be an emotional problem, an addiction, a relationship challenge, a money issue, illness. But it’s usually one theme over and over again. At some point we need to get the message: I can’t control the outer situation. I have to control my mind.

Lam Chung was struck by the realization that the dust he was constantly sweeping lacked true independent existence. Through meditating on this emptiness continuously, he attained complete liberation from suffering. He became a glorious arhat.

Lam Chung didn’t realize emptiness by sweeping. He combined the four powers and used sweeping as the opponent power. The object is a holy object — it’s a temple, a representation of Buddha’s pure land. He’s reciting a mantra. He’s got regret. So it’s doing some virtuous action with the four powers — that’s what’s purifying.

We can all take our jobs at the Dharma center and think: let me do my job as an opponent force and combine it with the four powers of purification.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: Lam Chung teaching the nuns; pure view of sangha
teaching.text:
Buddha directed his disciple Ananda to inform a certain community of nuns that their new spiritual guide was to be Lam Chung. The nuns were very upset — how can we accept as our abbot a monk who is so stupid? They decided to expose his inadequacies in public. They spread the word that a monk as wise as Buddha himself would be coming to give teachings, and even erected a large ostentatious throne without any steps.

When Lam Chung saw the throne without steps, he realized it had been constructed to make him look foolish. Without hesitation, he stretched out his hand like an enormous elephant’s trunk, reduced the throne to a small speck, returned it to its former size, and flew to the top of it. After a brief period of meditation, he flew into the sky and circled the gathering. Seated once more, he said: listen carefully, I will now give a week-long discourse on the meaning of one verse of Dharma. When the seven days of teaching were complete, many thousands attained a direct understanding of reality, while others attained stream-entry, once-returning, never-returning, and full arhat-ship. Buddha himself prophesied that Lam Chung would possess the greatest skill at taming the minds of others.

The nuns are a great mirror for us — when are we critical of our sangha friends? They’re seeing someone who’s realized emptiness, and they’re seeing him as a total loser. We can see a yogi as a loser. We don’t know anyone’s mind. Whenever we see a fellow sangha friend, we want to always have the purest view we can muster up. Any fault or imperfection we see, we just think: this is coming from my own mind.

We have amazing teachers here. Every teacher that teaches here is someone we should flock to their teachings. When we see them teach, we try to have a completely pure view of them, thinking, I’m getting teachings right from Buddha. We never want to discriminate between our teachers. We’re trying to get to a place where we can see everyone as a Buddha one day. A sangha friend who’s giving a dharma teaching, just speaking pure dharma words, is about as Buddha-like as it comes. At the very least, they must be functioning like an emanation in this moment.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: Skillful means and speech: three questions
teaching.text:
Lam Chung basically became this Buddha of skillful means, great skill in helping others. And Buddha showed great skill in helping Lam Chung by giving him that job.

One of the places we can improve our skill is in our speech. A teacher of mine who received this from Geshe-la taught this to me once. She said, we can ask: What do I have to share? What would be beneficial for this person? And what are they open to hearing?

These three questions are a great way to start practicing skillful speech. What do I have to share from my heart experientially? What would be beneficial for them to hear? And what are they actually open to hearing? In this Venn diagram, three circles — we find the intersection point.

Skillful means isn’t saying nothing. It’s not just being a secret Buddhist who says nothing. It does mean speaking and speaking up sometimes and saying our peace. But it’s doing so with these three considerations in mind. In this way, we can become skillful like Lam Chung.

Main point of all that: transform all of our activities into an opponent force by couching it in the other opponent powers.

announcements.speaker: Kadam Kyle
announcements.text: Let’s take a break now. We’ll come back at 6:15. Reminder — Kadam Morton’s going to be here Saturday teaching on the Middle Way, the union of karma and emptiness. We chose the most important subject on earth for him to teach on, since he’s a busy guy. It’s very kind of him to be here. And then the Backyard Blowout is the next day. Lots of good stuff coming up.

dedication.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dedication.text: Let’s dedicate now. Through the virtues we’ve collected through practicing, meditating, discussing — may all living beings find lasting peace of mind, enlightenment. We can make any personal prayers or dedications.

chantedPrayers.text: Liberating Prayer O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha, precious Treasury of Compassion, Bestower of Supreme Inner Peace. You who love all beings without exception are the source of happiness and goodness, and you guide us to the liberating path. Your body is a wish-fulfilling jewel, your speech is supreme, purifying nectar, and your mind is refuge for all living beings. With folded palms I turn to you, Supreme unchanging Friend. I request from the depths of my heart, please give me the light of your wisdom to dispel the darkness of my mind and to heal my mental continuum. Please nourish me with your goodness, that I in turn may nourish all beings with an unceasing banquet of delight. Through your compassionate intention, your blessings and virtuous deeds, and my strong wish to rely upon you, may all suffering quickly cease and all happiness and joy be fulfilled, and may holy Dharma flourish forevermore.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: MTB paragraphs 395–403: Opponent Force continued — doctor analogy, precipice, foolishness of neglecting Dharma
teaching.text:
If we need to comply with a doctor’s advice when frightened by a common illness, then is there any need to mention the necessity of listening to and following the spiritual advice of the most skilled physician, the compassionate Buddha? His powerful medicine of Dharma can cure the diseases that have plagued us since beginningless time — the poisonous delusions of attachment, anger, and ignorance.

Neither these nor the other pernicious world-consuming mental diseases can be cured by an ordinary doctor or his medicine. Only the great physician Buddha and his medicine of Dharma can overcome these diseases. If we do not take the remedy offered to us, where else can we possibly find relief? It is extremely foolish and ignorant to wish to be rid of samsaric suffering but to neglect the pursuit of spiritual practices.

If we need to be cautious when walking near the edge of a cliff, what need is there to mention the caution required near the edge of a precipice that drops down to the depths of hell? This is like a pit thousands of miles deep, and we are plunged into it for an extremely long time because of our creation of non-virtue.

It is unwise to think that we can enjoy ourselves today in the conviction that we will not die. No one has the power to say with confidence, death will not come to me today. Inevitably, there will be a time when we become nothing.

Shantideva concludes: Who can possibly say to me, “You have committed evil, but I will protect you”? No one. When I think that death is definite and the time of death is uncertain, how can I become free of this intense fear? The last line does not mean that we should never relax and enjoy ourselves. However, we should realize that at the present moment we have found a precious human life. To waste all our time engaged solely in the concerns of this lifetime is to lead a life no different from that of a dull-witted animal.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: Resistance to looking at suffering; why the Lam Rim renunciation sections are so long
teaching.text:
There is a resistance to looking at karmically created suffering and samsaric suffering. The renunciation section of the Lam Rim is the longest of all the meditations, and there’s like a two-page poem from Gung Thang just about aging.

Why is this section so long? It doesn’t let you leave it. Why is the birth section, the suffering of birth, so long? One reason is that there is a resistance to looking at it. Hopefully if it’s long enough, we stay in it long enough to let something move us. You might notice when you do that meditation, the sense of wanting to go faster through it — “Okay, let me move through this one.” That’s a sign of a bias in our mind that we have to notice and work through.

The analogies Geshe-la is giving here — walking near the edge of a cliff, getting an illness — they’re analogies trying to get us the sense that there is a danger. That feeling of literally being at the edge of a precipice, about to fall into a huge abyss. There is virtue there. If we don’t feel that way, it’s okay, but it’s a sign that there is this resistance to looking at suffering.

In the Mirror of Dharma presentation of the Lam Rim, we get four renunciation meditations out of the 15. We used to get one out of 21 on renunciation. Now we get four. Then there’s Danger of Lower Rebirth and Death, which are kind of renunciation meditations. We really get like six. Fantastic.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: MTB paragraphs 404–415: Power of Promise — types of promises, time periods, identity shift
teaching.text:
Power of Promise. The last of the four powers included in the confession of non-virtue is our firm promise never to repeat particular non-virtuous actions again. These four powers employed properly — it is certain that all our evil can be purified completely.

The power of the promise helps us purify the tendencies similar to the cause — the actions we keep performing that create the kind of negative karma we’re experiencing. By promising not to engage in them. When we make a promise, this is of a higher degree than just a wish or a desire. It’s best to make it to our spiritual guide and to all the Buddhas. Like a marriage vow — 100% I’m doing this.

There’s a range of promises. A promise that’s an intention: we’re promising to keep the intention to do something, not promising to do it. For example, a promise to keep an intention to be kind all day. These are easier to keep because it’s unlikely that we’d overtly break that. We might still be unkind, but it might not be because we had a strong intention to be unkind.

The other side is more specific: I’m going to do this, or I’m not going to do that. And then we apply a time to it. One minute. Ten minutes. One hour. One day. Whatever.

Sometimes people say, “I don’t want to make the promise because I’m afraid of breaking it.” This is just a cop-out. It’s a secret way of tricking ourselves to not change. Wisdom is thinking, how can I make the promise work? Not, how can I get out of doing this?

We don’t want to promise something too absurd, like never getting angry for a year. We need to know ourselves. But we can all make a promise that we can keep. Never think, I’m just not going to do anything because I’m afraid of breaking the promise. Be more afraid of not promising.

When we make the power of the promise, it’s helpful to think it through. What’s it going to look like? What could challenge it? What could break the promise? So if it’s, I’m not going to engage in hurtful speech for the next half a day — okay, what am I going to do when they push my buttons? We’re ensuring success by thinking it through ahead of time.

When we’re done with the promise, we want to bring a new person into that promise. We’re feeling like, okay, I’ve purified. Now I’m a different person. Now I’m going to live differently. We can view ourselves in a different role — more Buddha-like and pure, as a bodhisattva, a friend of the world, a Buddhist. Whatever it is. Because our identity usually precedes behavior: “I am this, so I do these kind of things.” If the identity hasn’t changed, it can be hard to change the behavior.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: MTB paragraphs 404–414: Substantial vs. circumstantial causes of karma
teaching.text:
In past lifetimes, we have been born in high positions, possessed beautiful forms, been endowed with great riches and wealth, experienced all the pleasures and joys of samsara, over and over again. However, as Shantideva says, what remains of those experiences now? They are empty of meaning.

We have many wrong views concerning our pleasures and comforts. We generally think all our possessions and wealth have come about as a result of our own efforts in this lifetime. “I’m a clever investor.” No. It has nothing to do with that. There are many cleverer investors who are dead broke, or dead, or in jail.

We should realize that there are two kinds of cause for all our experiences: the substantial cause was created in a previous life or earlier in this life, while the circumstantial causes are the conditions occurring in this life that bring the substantial cause to fruition.

A rich man may well have worked very hard to become wealthy, but the work he did is still only a circumstantial cause. The main substantial cause was the practice of giving during a previous lifetime.

The two brothers who go into the same business independently — same parents, same education, same capital — one meets with great success, the other goes bankrupt. Both created the proper circumstantial causes, so why different results? Because the substantial cause — the practice of giving — was created by only one of the brothers.

A person with a digestive problem falls ill. The circumstantial cause was the food he ate, but the substantial cause was some non-virtuous action committed previously. If he had not created that substantial cause, even if he ate food that gave others indigestion, he would never experience the suffering himself — like a peacock who eats poisonous plants and grows stronger.

Shantideva summarizes: All suffering arises from non-virtue; all happiness arises from virtue. Thus, throughout the day and the night, I must consider how I can be free from non-virtue, the source of all misery. This concludes Disclosure of Evil, the second chapter of the text Meaningful to Behold.

teaching.speaker: David
teaching.text:
A couple years ago I did tons of Vajrasattva mantras, and one question is: if you do a regular purification practice, does it make sense to just stick with the same promise? I remember promising to make effort towards opposing my anger and annoyance. And I feel like I haven’t made the type of progress I would have liked to. I think I am probably a little bit less angry — but I still get angry every single day basically, unless I’m up at the temple. That’s the only time I can go 24 hours without getting annoyed.

The role thing would help, but as I picture doing this, it doesn’t feel different enough. I did it for like a year and it didn’t work. So I’m looking for new solutions or a fresh way of approaching it.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: The mind as an interconnected network; why lingering on one meditation doesn’t work
teaching.text:
Yeah, with a situation like this, the mind is like a network — an interconnected network of little points, each with weights and nodes that all relate to one another. Often, if we’re really hammering on something and it doesn’t seem to be going somewhere, it’s probably being dragged down by a bunch of other stuff. We’re hammering away at this little anger node, but it’s supported by things elsewhere — not understanding karma sufficiently, not having enough renunciation, not thinking about the good qualities of suffering, insufficient compassion.

If we’re really working on something and it’s obviously not moving, it’s probably a sign that there’s another blockage in the network. We’re misallocating our resources to that one node and not the other very important points.

This is why the Lam Rim is so helpful — it makes sure we don’t do this. By hitting all the Lam Rim minds, we keep building up the whole network, because they’re all stacked on each other. If one is very weak, it will drag down the entire system. The system will not budge until that budges. Unless we have this holistic approach to our mind, it doesn’t particularly move very well.

We can do these little projects and they’re great, especially if there’s a weakness somewhere. But we don’t want to be so focused on one project that we’re ignoring the rest of the network. It’s a sign like, okay, you did enough on that, but there’s probably other places that would be more interesting and higher leverage to interact with.

teaching.speaker: Grady
teaching.text:
This section is coming up at the perfect time for me. We just came off a weekend where we met some people who weren’t close friends — when we moved, we let the relationship dissipate. We ran into them this weekend. So next week, I’m finding out that we’re attending a party that is another old relationship resurfacing. This one’s more poignant — very old, very close friend. The relationship fell apart, and I think there were hurt feelings that I probably had some things to do with. I might be the reason it fell apart.

I’ve harbored a lot of guilt for a long time about it. And it’s coming up next week. I’ve tried to purify it, but I haven’t seen him, so it’s easy to go, oh, I’m good because I don’t see him. Now I’m like — who am I going to be for him and for me? I’m unprepared. Any help would be great.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.note: Approaching emotionally difficult situations as spiritual opportunities; wisdom planning; funneling raw feeling into bodhichitta
teaching.text:
These kind of experiences are very, very spiritually meaningful — trying to make something right that was wrong. There’s something about it that involves a lot of selflessness if we can come at it from the right point of view. Because it’s doing something that our ego wouldn’t want to do at all. It can be awkward or strange or difficult. But it’s fantastic for liberating us from samsara — to go into this emotionally dangerous setting that would be easy to just avoid, but instead going in there, sword brandished, running into battle to practice dharma.

So the first thing is to impute like this: this is very good spiritually for me. It is awkward and incredibly uncomfortable, but it’s very good spiritually for me. That view really changes the whole dynamic.

Second, in these kind of situations, it’s really nice to do some extra planning — wisdom planning. With your spiritual guide, with sangha friends. Like, when they say this, what will I say? What if they’re really mad and give me the cold shoulder? What’s my practice for that? What if they seem like everything is fine? This isn’t overthinking — it’s wisdom planning. Like how you’d approach a job interview. You think through all the decision trees. And then you’re ready.

Last thing: take the feeling of letting someone down and try to find what virtue it can funnel into. That feeling is incredibly raw and awful — it just crushes us. But every feeling can be funneled into a virtuous mind. With letting people down, it’s really bodhichitta fodder. Why? Because until we’re a Buddha, we will forever let people down. Forever. We’re completely hallucinating a false world, completely plagued by delusions. That’s a painful thing to acknowledge. But when we’re in one of those moments, we can try to ride it into a virtue — the virtue of bodhichitta. Thinking, until I’m a Buddha, I will forever let people down. And we use it as a spiritual gift that will propel us to Buddhahood.

pairedDiscussion.note: Paired discussion removed. Audio garbled in both Whale and Dolphin. David read pairs: Mary Ann and Anne P, Mimi and Sumit, David and Anne K, Jose and Suzanne, and Alexis, Fran, and Dale (trio).

practiceDiscussion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceDiscussion.text: What should we emphasize for these next two months?

practiceDiscussion.speaker: Alexis
practiceDiscussion.text: Based on our fabulous conversation — the thing that’s just this hamster wheel going on and on and on — I’m just purifying that, the four-step process, doing what you said about the Lam Rim and using the Lam Rim as an opponent force. That’s what I’m doing until I go to the next one.

practiceDiscussion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceDiscussion.text: Very nice. So you’re going to take a specific kind of repetitive karmic pattern, target it with your purification practice — the four powers — and the main opponent force you’re going to use is the Lam Rim meditation each day. Fantastic. That’ll be great for two months. That’ll do you real good.

practiceDiscussion.speaker: Fran
practiceDiscussion.text: Besides continuing my efforts to purify my lack of concentration, in the break I really want to work on recognizing Dharma opportunities throughout the day.

practiceDiscussion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceDiscussion.text: Yeah, it really is such a core Kadampa practice — bringing daily appearances into the path. Geshe-la said, one day when we can do that with everything, then we will live in a Lam Rim pure land. Which is very similar to an actual pure land. Because everything would just be a virtuous object for us — completely concentrated and peaceful all the time, because everything just teaches us Lam Rim.

practiceDiscussion.speaker: Sumit
practiceDiscussion.text: I think many of us are going to do HYT, and I think we should really do the tantric version of this, of purification — the four purities about enjoyments and so forth. I know that’s not really covered in this book exactly, but I think if you’re about to do HYT, it really behooves you to do that. Engaging in that form of purification and still do the thing you said in your daily life — the tantric stuff really applies to the daily life stuff. Bringing the tantric purities in.

practiceDiscussion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceDiscussion.text:
Yeah, Sumit is referring to the fact that every complete tantric practice has to contain four complete purities: purity of body or self, environment, activities, and enjoyments. Body or self is who we are. Environment is where we live. Activities is what we do. Enjoyments is where we look for pleasure.

Our samsaric situation is basically: an ordinary person in a suffering world — that’s the environment. What do we do? Just follow self-cherishing and delusion. What do we enjoy? We enjoy things in a way that creates attachment. Every tantric practice has to include ways to purify all four of these facets of our samsara. Our tantric practice is definitely our most vital purification that we do.

Geshe-la said once: what is Buddha? Buddha is just complete purity. That’s all Buddha is.

practiceDiscussion.speaker: Grady
practiceDiscussion.text: My practice is pretty clear for the next week. I’ll report in. I’ll give you the analysis after it happens.

conclusion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
conclusion.text:
Okay, I think that’s everything. So, exam in a few weeks. I sent out the questions today on WhatsApp. I’ll just choose five of those. Should be easy peasy, lemon squeezy, as they say. Just enjoy — enjoy having Meaningful to Behold in your heart. Well, one fourth of it. It should be lovely. We can see each other either next weekend or in a couple of months.

Okay, let’s just dedicate here. We can think through the virtues we’ve collected through practicing, meditating, discussing. May all living beings find lasting peace of mind, enlightenment. And we can make any personal prayers or dedications.
